3.title: Deploy a Cloudflare Worker from Replit – anytime, anywhere
3.author: Replit Blog
3.description:
From large-scale businesses to nonprofits to anyone on the Internet, Cloudflare aims to make developer applications faster, more secure and more reliable. Cloudflare also offers an entire suite of developer products to help build the fundamental pieces of their applications. Every day, thousands of new developers around the world use the Cloudflare Developer Platform offerings from compute to storage to opinionated developer products to deploy everything from serverless functions to full-stack applications.

With the Cloudflare Developer Platform’s mission to meet developers where they are, today, we’re excited to announce that you can now deploy Cloudflare Workers (serverless functions) from Replit! Easily deploy a Worker to Cloudflare’s global network and manage your projects anytime, anywhere and from any device. With Replit, you can experience a streamlined onboarding experience and setup with just a few clicks.

"We've been hearing from our users that they want a way to deploy to Cloudflare Workers with Replit. We're very excited about this template and to collaborate with Cloudflare to make it easier for developers building on Replit to use whatever technologies they choose.” — Bardia Pourvakil, Head of Developer Relations at Replit

What are Cloudflare Workers?

4.title: Celebrating 20 Million Replit Developers
4.author: Replit Blog
4.description:
Today, we celebrate 20 million developers on Replit. They've created 240M+ Repls, ranging from multiplayer games to production software with the power of real-time collaboration in the cloud and state-of-the-art AI tools. Developers build their businesses on Replit too, from indie hackers to YC-backed startups like Fig, AmpleMarket, and BerriAI to unicorns like Deel.



The Replit Story

In 2010, I was a young hacker in Amman, Jordan. I didn't have my own computer, but coding was my life. I’d go to internet cafés or borrow computers, and every time I switched machines, I needed to set up a new development environment from scratch. Worse, I couldn’t save my progress or collaborate with my friends. I’d email myself and others my code so we could work on different machines.

Around that time, Google Docs came out, and it struck me that nothing like it existed for programming. I became obsessed with an idea: to create a world where I could open a browser tab, start coding, write a runnable program, collaborate with others, and access my work from any other device.

5.title: AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about?
5.author: Dolphia
5.description:
As more product work is generated from shared patterns, designers need to decide where an experience should surprise, celebrate, or simply leave someone alone.

Imagine asking an AI tool to design a task-completion state.

The result has a checkmark, a friendly message, and a small burst of confetti. It uses the right components. The spacing matches the system. The animation is polished.

Now imagine that same response after two different tasks.

In one, someone has finished setting up a business they have spent months trying to launch. In the other, an administrator has updated the forty-seventh record of the morning.

The component is consistent. The experiences should probably be different.

Nothing in the confetti explains which moment deserves it. That decision depends on what the person has done, how often they do it, and whether they want the product to make an occasion of it.

As AI becomes more capable of assembling interfaces from established patterns, this distinction deserves more attention. We are getting better at telling tools what belongs to our product. We also need to decide what belongs to the moment.

Matching the system is an incomplete definition of quality

There are good reasons to care about consistency. People should not have to relearn familiar actions on every screen. Teams should not spend their time reconstructing decisions already made elsewhere.

Figma’s guidance on working with its agent describes how components, guidelines, examples, and task-specific context help generated work reflect a team’s product. That is useful progress. It also makes clear that consistency depends on the context supplied to the tool.

But a faithful rendering of a system can still be an emotionally inappropriate response.

A success message can be correct and patronizing. An illustration can match the brand and occupy space someone needs for their work. A playful loading state can be charming until it appears during a time-sensitive task.

These failures are difficult to identify by inspecting the component alone. They emerge from the relationship between the component and the person encountering it.

In my earlier article about design-system judgment, I explored the distinction between enforcing rules and deciding whether a pattern is appropriate. Expression brings another version of that problem into view: a detail can follow every rule we wrote and still misunderstand the occasion.

I want software to have room for color, humor, beauty, and small surprises.

I want an interaction to feel satisfying, even when satisfaction cannot be reduced to a shorter completion time.

I also want the product to recognize when I have work to do.

Pleasure has a history beyond the AI conversation

Designers were studying this long before generative interfaces.

Don Norman’s work on emotional design considers appearance, the experience of using something, and the meaning people attach to it. That gives us a broader vocabulary than “add delight.” Pleasure can come from how something looks, how well it responds, or what owning and using it means to someone.

Therese Fessenden’s distinction between surface and deep delight is useful here too. An amusing detail can create a moment of pleasure, while a well-considered workflow can produce a quieter satisfaction that lasts through the task.

The second does not make the first disposable.

A product can be dependable and exuberant. A useful tool can have a peculiar illustration or a lovely transition simply because someone cared about making it enjoyable. We do not have to defend every expressive choice by pretending it saves three seconds.

But we do have to understand what it asks of the person.

A color choice might make a screen more inviting without adding a step. A celebration might demand attention. A joke might require cultural familiarity. A transition might make a relationship easier to understand — or force someone to wait.

“Delight” is too generous a label to apply before finding out which of those things happened.

A playful product still needs restraint

Duolingo offers an instructive example because expression is already central to its identity.

In its account of redesigning the app’s core tabs, the team describes experimenting with several visual directions, then finding tensions between consistency and purpose. An illustrated header on every tab created uniformity, but some illustrations occupied space without communicating anything useful.

The solution included different header sizes for different purposes, with titles kept in consistent positions.

That is a more useful lesson than “make every screen playful.” A recognizable product can vary its emphasis while preserving familiar structure. The team’s own account shows that even an expressive brand needs to ask where an illustration earns its space.

This matters when a design becomes an example for AI to reuse.

If the reference screen has a large illustration, should the next screen have one too? Is the illustration a general rule, a possibility, or a response to a particular situation?

A tool can reproduce the visible answer while missing the reason for it. So can a designer working from an incomplete specification.

As generation becomes easier, that missing explanation can travel further. A choice made for one meaningful moment becomes the default for several ordinary ones.

The expressive detail survives. Its purpose does not.

Consistency can include a change in tone

Mailchimp’s voice-and-tone guidance makes an important distinction: its voice remains recognizable, while its tone responds to the reader’s circumstances.

The guide welcomes humor but gives clarity priority. It asks writers to consider whether someone has finished a campaign or is confused and looking for help, and warns against forcing a joke.

This is a practical way to preserve personality without requiring the same emotional performance everywhere.

A product’s identity can live in how sensitively it changes.

Warmth during onboarding might mean encouragement. Warmth after an error might mean a direct explanation, preserved work, and a clear next step. The writing can sound like the same company without treating both situations as opportunities for comedy.

That distinction should also shape instructions given to AI.

“Make it friendly and playful” leaves a great deal unresolved. Friendly to whom? Playful at what point? What has just happened?

A more useful instruction describes the situation: the user’s work is safe; they need to understand why the action failed; avoid humor; make the recovery path obvious.

There is still room for good writing within those constraints. The constraints establish what the writing owes the person.

Expression can make an interface clearer

It is tempting to organize this debate as a negotiation between expressive design and usable design. Google’s research on Material 3 Expressive complicates that framing.

In its published research account, Google describes an email interface where the Send button became larger, more prominent, and closer to the keyboard. Participants located it faster. The expressive treatment also changed hierarchy and placement; its benefit cannot be attributed to decoration alone.

The same report includes a less successful experiment: a playlist replaced familiar rows with a scattered arrangement of album artwork. Participants found it visually exciting, but usability suffered.

These are findings from Google’s tested designs, not evidence that every product should adopt the same aesthetic. Together, they show why the actual interaction matters more than the adjective attached to it.

Color can establish emphasis. Shape can distinguish actions. Motion can show where something went. An expressive decision may help people understand a product while making it more pleasurable.

The question is what remains legible after we introduce it.

A familiar control can carry considerable character. A surprising arrangement can remove the very cues someone needs to use it. Designers have to examine both effects, rather than accepting “on brand” or “more delightful” as sufficient explanations.

The same delight can become someone else’s interruption

Asana’s celebrations show why preference belongs in this discussion.

Its 2016 introduction of an expanded celebration system described occasional animated characters appearing after task completion, with celebrations enabled through settings.

A 2018 community discussion captures the other side: a customer found the characters intrusive and asked how to disable them. A reply explained the setting.

That exchange does not establish how most users felt. It does show that the same detail can be welcome to one person and unwelcome to another.

This is where the word “delight” can hide an assumption. We describe our intention as though it were already the user’s response.

A celebration designed to recognize accomplishment may become an obstacle during repetitive work. Something enjoyed privately may feel inappropriate during a presentation. Someone may like the character and still prefer to finish without watching it.

Giving people control is part of designing the experience well.

For motion, the stakes can extend beyond preference. W3C’s guidance for Animation from Interactions, a Level AAA criterion, explains why people need ways to disable nonessential interaction-triggered movement, including the potential for vestibular symptoms.

An expressive experience should have a considered reduced-motion version. Removing movement should leave clear feedback, meaningful hierarchy, and an understandable result.

There are many ways to make something feel good. Movement is one of them.

AI changes how easily the wrong detail can spread

None of these problems began with AI. Teams have copied patterns without understanding them for years.

What AI introduces is another way to reproduce those decisions — and an opportunity to be more explicit about them.

A library might describe a celebration’s colors, duration, and animation curve. That describes the asset. It says little about whether a celebration should happen after someone completes a tutorial, pays a bill, or removes an account.

Those are different events even if the system labels all three “success.”

Here is a hypothetical rule worth testing: a fuller acknowledgment for a meaningful first achievement; brief feedback for repeated routine actions; direct, restrained language for sensitive outcomes.

That rule will not fit every product. Its value is that it gives the team something concrete to question.

Is the first achievement actually meaningful to the person, or merely valuable to our onboarding metrics? Does a repeated action become meaningful when it completes a larger goal? Are we assuming we know how someone feels because we know which button they pressed?

A good specification should leave those questions visible.

AI can help explore expressive alternatives: different copy, motion treatments, layouts, and levels of emphasis. There is no need to claim that surprise or beauty belongs exclusively to human production.

But producing an alternative and establishing when it is welcome are different kinds of work.

If we evaluate generated interfaces mainly by how closely they match the library, we will favor what is easiest to compare. If we ask whether the experience suits the occasion, we need examples, use over time, and feedback from the people living with it.

That is a broader evaluation than a screenshot review can provide.

“Worth caring about” should not mean harder to leave

There is another complication: products can use expression to serve goals people did not choose.

A cheerful character might encourage a useful habit. It might also make declining an offer feel like disappointing someone. A reward animation might acknowledge progress, or distract from how little progress actually occurred.

Those possibilities need to remain in the argument. Emotional design is capable of persuasion as well as pleasure.

The appropriate question is whose purpose the detail advances.

Does it help someone enjoy an activity they value? Does it acknowledge something they accomplished? Or does it make the product’s preferred behavior harder to refuse?

Time spent and repeat visits cannot answer that on their own. Someone may return because the product is useful, because leaving is costly, or because a mechanic creates pressure. Those explanations have different implications for design.

I am interested in software people appreciate using. That requires taking their ability to dislike a detail seriously, even when it is the detail the team loves most.

Give the expressive decision a proper review

In a product team, this work needs a place before the final polish pass.

For a proposed expressive moment, I would want to see it in three conditions: the first encounter, repeated use, and a situation where the person is rushed or something has gone wrong.

The same animation may behave beautifully in isolation and become tiring in a sequence. The same line of copy may be reassuring on a quiet afternoon and dismissive during a failure.

Research should make room for those differences. Watch whether people can continue. Ask what they think the response means. Find out whether they want to see it again. Include people who prefer less motion or sound, and test whether the experience still communicates clearly.

These observations will not produce a universal delight score. They can help us distinguish a detail people value from one they tolerate.

This also changes what we document.

Alongside the approved example, record the circumstance it serves, when to scale it back, and a case where it should not be used. Give both people and AI tools a reason to choose differently.

A system with that kind of guidance can protect character. It can make room for an unusual illustration, a distinctive rhythm, or a moment of celebration while keeping everyday work dependable.

The alternative is to encode only what is easy to repeat and hope the rest survives delivery.

I want the products we build with AI to have more room for pleasure: a color choice that lifts a screen, a response that acknowledges effort, a transition that feels unusually right. I also want that pleasure to survive actual use, beyond the first demo and the designer’s own preferences.

Return to the two completed tasks. The new business owner and the administrator may both need confirmation. One might welcome a moment to take in what they have accomplished. The other might want the next record ready.

AI can generate both responses.

We still have to notice that the occasions are different.

AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

6.title: What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us
6.author: Anna Lefour
6.description:
Three design experts told me how AI is changing the way we build and maintain Design Systems. And led me to think that “the future” is already happening now.

You’ve probably read, or even written, one of those LinkedIn posts about someone building a complete Design System in 20 minutes with Claude. Or in 15 minutes with Gemini. Or… you get the idea.

Those posts made me curious. I had never built a full Design System, although I had set up the basic elements of one before I really dug into AI, and it was as interesting as it was painful. So the promise of building a full one in minutes was appealing.

My mistake? Confusing a UI kit with a Design System, and believing the whole process could really be done in minutes.

At UXDX Berlin last May, two talks about Design Systems made me want to know more about how AI has changed them in the day-to-day of product teams. That curiosity led me to interview three design experts, and to get to the essential part of what a Design System actually is: Marianne Ashton-Booth, Head of Product Design at ITV; David Sward, Chief Design Officer at Siemens; and Nicolas Chatelain, freelance Senior Designer and specialized in Design System and Ops.

Three experts, three different approaches. Nicolas Chatelain bets on a frame that bends without breaking, flexible with teams and ready for AI. David Sward bets on speed with guardrails, with AI as a tool and a human in the loop. Marianne Ashton-Booth bets on people and process, treating the Design System like a product.

The last two had both just given a talk at UXDX when I talked with them, so what follows draws on two different moments with each of them: what they said on stage, and what they told me one-on-one afterwards.

1. AI automates the easy part, but the hard part still belongs to humans

One-on-one after her talk, Marianne Ashton-Booth said something that felt particularly on point to me: “Anybody can spin up prototypes in minutes, and that’s great. But then that gap between what’s actually feasible, what’s actually close to the brand, or close to the actual components that we’ve got, can be quite distant.”

Nicolas Chatelain, whom I interviewed in July, put the same idea in other words: the UI is the easy part of a Design System. “The hardest part, the one that makes a DS work or not, is governance and adoption.”

Neither of them sees the components as the problem; Nicolas even says anyone could, indeed, build a kit while we were talking. What matters is consistency across teams, and across a whole company, and that is the human part of a Design System. A Zeroheight report on the state of Design Systems, published in early 2026, points the same way: 59% of practitioners credit communication and community for their system’s adoption.

On stage, Marianne Ashton-Booth had already named what breaks instead. When a design system fails, she said, “it’s almost never just [the design system’s core operations]. The components are usually fine.” What breaks are the invisible layers underneath: trust, communication, prioritisation, relationships, and shared belief.

2. The bottleneck has moved from production speed to review

“My biggest problem is trying to slow people down with AI,” David Sward told me. Indeed, AI has sped up a lot of processes, all the way to delivery.

Here, he does not mean slowing his team down so that they get used to AI, but keeping them inside the security and compliance rules of a large enterprise. With hundreds of products relying on his system, a mistake would take several hundred million euros to fix. His operating principle: “don’t break things.”

But the fact remains: productivity has risen. And once speed is there, the bottleneck shifts from production to the people who review, validate and keep everything coherent. Nicolas Chatelain and Marianne Ashton-Booth ran into this too.

During Nicolas Chatelain’s mission for an international group, for example, AI-boosted product teams started to outpace the central Design System team, whose original strategy was to lock everything down. His verdict:

“With AI, it’s a total rollback. We have to become much more flexible, because tomorrow people could create a kit in five minutes. If we become useless, they’ll find an even easier way to bypass us.”

Figma’s slots, which let teams put their own content inside a standardised component, are one way to loosen the frame.

At ITV, Marianne Ashton-Booth’s team takes another route and relies on “design system reps” in both design and engineering: “They tend to be the go-to people that have a little bit more prominence and involvement in things like final decisions. It just means that things can keep moving rather than just becoming a bit of a bottleneck.” On stage, she added that rather than treating AI as a separate topic, ITV asked the right question: “What does that mean for the design system? How should our processes evolve?”

These three approaches suggest that there is no single way to handle the bottleneck: it depends on the context, the level of risk, and how far AI has advanced, and been accepted, in the organisation. That is precisely where humans remain useful: understanding at what moment, and to what extent, everyone who holds decision-making power over the Design System should step in, and when they should let go.

3. The Design System is becoming something AI reads

This is the part that sounds most like “the future”, but is actually already the present: making the system readable for machines.

Nicolas Chatelain’s team started watching tools like V0 and Lovable in the second half of 2025, and concluded it was too early to adopt them. They chose to prepare the system instead: tokens migrated to the DTCG (Design Tokens Community Group) standard, a shared format for the values of a system, like colours, spacing or typography, so that every tool, and every AI agent, reads them the same way.

An MCP server (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI agent query the Design System directly, for instance to find the right component or token, instead of guessing. In a field study published in July 2026, Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent looked at 21 open-source Design Systems: 20 of them offer an MCP server (official or community-built), but only 3 have set up Figma Code Connect, which ties a Figma component to its real code counterpart. Plenty of systems let AI read them, far fewer tie their components back to design.

David Sward’s team uses AI on the other side of the process: a large language model (LLM) compares what teams have implemented with what the Design System is supposed to be, and, in his words, “systematically tells you what to fix.” In his own Design System, AI stays “a tool just like anything else” (an engine harmonises thousands of icons, for instance), and his broader principle holds: “You can’t remove a human from the loop and then expect them to step back in to operate the system if they don’t understand the state the system is in.”

Marianne Ashton-Booth, on her end, is adamant: “There might be parts of [a design system] that become more AI-generated or automated. But a design system isn’t just that part, you know, it’s the people and it’s the process as well. And that’s the bit that I think we’ll still retain.”

Where I think we’re heading: code as the source of truth

These insights led me to believe this is where Design Systems are heading: the code, rather than the design file, is becoming their source of truth. We might already be there. Designers who use AI seem to open Figma less and less (that’s my case), and in teams where shipping and iterating beat perfecting details, the blurring of roles (I talked about it here) doesn’t help.

Nicolas Chatelain said it: “Today, the source of truth has to be the code. Absolutely.” Working in the code removes a layer of abstraction between AI and production, and “tomorrow, when this documentation lives directly in the code, we won’t need Figma anymore.” He admits he may be “completely wrong”, and still finds Figma useful to explore and fine-tune. And I agree with him that Figma isn’t dead. But for me its place in the process has definitely changed.

Concretely, it means that whatever is merged into the code becomes the standard, and design files, documentation and AI agents all read from it. Every review then becomes a governance decision. But as Tony Ward wrote in his recent article “Code as the Source of Truth”, the key is to keep “a subject-matter expert in the loop at every step of the way.” Which leaves the real question: in this new process, who gets to say what goes into the truth?

As for me, meeting these three experts showed me there is no single answer to that question. Each built theirs from their own environment, and in that richness I found keys to meet my own challenges. I hope you will too.

Thanks to UXDX for providing access to the event, and to David Sward, Marianne Ashton-Booth and Nicolas Chatelain for their time.

All of Nicolas Chatelain’s quotes were translated from French.

What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

7.title: In a world of panic, calm and certainty win
7.author: Dan Maccarone
7.description:
While panic around what AI means for our industry is the reflex right now, calm is a decision. The calm that comes from knowing what you actually know is the rarest and most valuable thing you can bring to a moment like this.

I recently turned 50 and reckoning with that did what it does to so many people. It made me think. Not in a hauntingly dramatic, staring-out-the-window way, but in an introspective way where you start taking stock of what you’ve actually learned, what still rattles you, and what has stopped rattling you entirely.

That thinking rooted itself from a conversation I had with Skift founder Rafat Ali. When he found out my birthday was coming, he got genuinely excited for me, which is not how most people react to 50. He told me the day after my birthday would be the best day of my life, because that’s when you get to put the whole thing behind you. He said that you just stop carrying the pressure you put on yourself and the pressure you imagine everyone else is putting on you.

That conversation quickly moved on from my age and on to work, to his industry and to what AI is doing to all of it. Without noticing, Rafat said the same thing again in a completely different context.

“There’s so much uncertainty,” he told me, “that the people who stay calm and certain are the ones everyone listens to. In a moment where nobody knows what’s happening, calm is the whole advantage.”

I haven’t stopped thinking about that since.

Those two pieces of advice are actually one piece of advice. The relief Rafat promised me about 50, the freedom of putting down the need to prove yourself, is the exact thing that makes a person valuable in a moment like this one.

The whole industry is panicking about AI. The people who come out of it fine will be the ones who already learned how to put the panic down.

The fear is real

The numbers are striking.

Pew Research found that 71 percent of Americans now think AI will mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, up from 64 percent two years earlier, and among adults under 30 it’s 73 percent. Pew is careful to note that number reflects what people expect, not jobs that have actually been lost.

ADP’s global study of more than thirty-nine thousand people, led by their chief economist Nela Richardson, found that anxiety, not confidence, is now the defining feeling workers have about their work.

A survey from the Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center found nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest polled.

It has gotten real enough that it’s showing up in doctors’ offices. Dr. Simbiat Adighije described a patient who couldn’t stop checking the news, couldn’t stop imagining which parts of her job and her identity might be automated next, and made a point worth holding onto

The anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it ever comes true, the same way climate anxiety is legitimate no matter what you think of any particular model.

This isn’t in your head. The ground is actually moving, and anyone who says otherwise is lying to your face.

Look closely at that Pew number, though, because it’s quite telling. The dread is at an all-time high, and it’s a forecast, a thing people expect, running well ahead of what has actually happened to them. That gap, between how frightened people are and what has actually changed in their own working lives, is where panic lives.

Fear and panic are not the same thing. Fear is a reasonable response to a real risk. Panic is what happens when the fear starts making your decisions for you.

The clinical psychologist Zachary Sikora says that fear is literally our survival response, useful, hardwired, and designed to keep us alive. When it spikes, however, it impairs the part of the brain that handles reasoning and judgment, the exact faculties you need most when things are uncertain.

The more afraid you get, the worse you think.

We have seen this exact panic before

Every big technological shift runs the same arc.

Dora Czerna traced it across decades of disruptions and named the stages. First comes democratization, when a tool suddenly lets a lot more people do something that used to take an expert. Then comes panic, when the experts realize it. Then a stretch of genuine quality collapse, when all those new people flood the zone with mediocre work. Eventually, new norms settle in, and the field is bigger and different and mostly fine.

When desktop publishing arrived, it gave us a decade of ransom-note flyers with twelve fonts on them, and then it gave us a generation of designers who could do more than any typesetter ever could.

The panic comes for everyone. Whether you give in to it is up to you.

This isn’t simply a modern problem. Calestous Juma, who spent years studying how societies react to new technology, found the same pattern running back six hundred years. Coffee, refrigeration, mechanized farming, electricity, every one of them met a wave of fear and resistance before it became ordinary.

The fear, he found, was rarely really about the technology, but rather about people sensing they might lose a piece of their identity or their livelihood, feeling it first and reaching for the evidence afterward.

Economist Derek Thompson has pointed out that the single strongest argument for AI not causing some overnight jobs apocalypse is one word, history. New technology has been reshaping work for centuries, and the story is always the same. The technology shows up, the work changes, and it almost always goes slower and messier than anyone predicted in the panic.

I’ve certainly experienced my own smaller versions of this. The web was going to make everyone a designer, and then it didn’t. The bootcamps were going to flood the field and end the profession, and then they didn’t.

Every time this happens, the panic feels like the end of something, and every time it turns out to be the loud, ugly middle of something, the part right before the new normal shows up and everyone forgets they were ever that scared.

Panic in a downturn is the go-to emotion, even at the top. Nancy Koehn, who studies how leaders handle crises, points to research showing that more than half of leaders become more closed-minded and controlling when a crisis hits, and more than four in ten get angrier and more reactive. The steadiness we remember in the leaders who got it right, the Lincolns and the Shackletons, was always the rare response, which is exactly why it resonates so well.

None of this means the fear is wrong. It means the fear is a stage, and stages pass, especially for the people who don’t let it take over.

The calm that wins is the kind you earn

There’s a version of calm that’s just denial, the person insisting nothing is changing while the ground shifts under them. Plugging your ears with your fingers, screaming “la la la la la,” hoping the phase just passes you by.

That’s not what Rafat was describing in our conversation. The calm that actually wins is the kind you earn, the kind that comes from knowing what you’re good at, having done the work enough times to trust your own informed point-of-view, and no longer needing to prove any of it to anyone.

ADP’s global study found that the workers using AI the most heavily reported significantly less stress than the ones barely touching it, about half as many said they felt overloaded.

Ethan Mollick has been saying for years that the people who get their hands on AI, who learn its edges and its failures firsthand, are the ones who stop fearing it and start using it well.

Familiarity is what turns a vague threat into a known quantity. The dread lives in the gap between you and the thing you’re afraid of.

Patrick Neeman argues that the way out of AI anxiety is to trade the vague fear, the sense that you’re falling behind because everyone else seems to get it, for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work. Vague is the natural state of panic. Specific is the natural state of calm.

The discomfort of being visibly bad at something new, Neeman writes, is just the cost of staying in the game.

This is where Rafat Ali’s point-of-view comes back in, because it turns out his advice wasn’t a passing mood. Ali actually built his whole company around it. When he relaunched Skift in September 2026, he wrote that AI is making information cheaper every month and judgment more valuable, and the three things that never get cheaper are knowledge nobody else has, a point of view on what it means, and access to the people who make the decisions.

The calm he promised me and the strategy he bet his company on are the same thing. Both come from being secure in the one thing the machine can’t hand you.

In a moment when no one is sure what’s happening, the calm, informed person doesn’t just steady themselves, they become the one everyone else steadies against. That is the oldest definition of leadership there is.

The reason panic is such a bad trade is that it spends all your energy on the part you can’t control, the speed of the technology, and none on the part you can, the judgment you bring to it.

The future is a design problem

There’s a specific cost to the panic that most people miss.

Gallup found that when a worker crosses over into believing their job is likely to be eliminated, their engagement drops, their burnout climbs, their satisfaction falls, and they become measurably more likely to start looking for the exit. The belief does the damage, often well before the technology does anything at all.

Panic is not a neutral way to wait out a storm. It quietly degrades the exact things, your focus, your judgment, your work, that you’d need to come through it well.

The real question is what you do with the uncertainty instead. Economist David Autor argues that the AI future should not be not treated as a prediction exercise, but rather as a design problem,.

We tend to talk about what’s coming as though it’s weather, something to forecast and brace for. Autor’s point is that we have enormous say in how it actually goes, through the choices we make and the things we decide to build.

The future isn’t something you wait to find out. It’s something you have a hand in making.

Economists aren’t the only ones saying this. Carolyn Dewar, who advises chief executives at McKinsey, bluntly says that AI won’t decide the future, the people leading through it will.

That’s really a description of what leadership has always been. The best leaders stay calm when no one else does. They get informed instead of getting loud, and they keep making clear-eyed decisions while everyone around them spins out.

A moment of maximum uncertainty is exactly when that kind of person becomes most valuable.

Panic is abdication. Calm, informed, and decisive drives success.

That is the difference between panic and calm. One treats the future as weather, something you brace for and can’t change. The other treats it as a problem, which is a thing you already know how to handle.

Which brings me back to Rafat Ali and to the thing he told me about turning 50. The relief he promised was finally putting away the weight of trying to prove you belong, and discovering that what’s left underneath is everything you actually know how to do. That’s the same calm that wins right now, the calm of someone who has stopped bracing for the future and started building their small corner of it.

You can spend this moment frightened of what AI might take from you or you can get quiet, take stock of what you actually bring, and go to work.The people who come through this just fine are already doing the second thing. They put the panic down, and they got back to the part that was always theirs.

References and further reading

The fear is real

  • Pew Research Center, Americans Are Increasingly Wary of AI. The survey finding that 71 percent of Americans expect AI to mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, rising to 73 percent among adults under 30.
  • Nela Richardson and ADP Research, Today at Work. A global study of more than thirty-nine thousand workers finding that anxiety, not confidence, now defines how people feel about their jobs.
  • Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center, The AI Anxiety Era. A survey finding nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest.
  • Dr. Simbiat Adighije, Anticipatory Anxiety About AI Is Showing Up in Clinic (KevinMD). A psychiatrist on treating patients for AI dread, and why the anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it comes true.
  • Zachary Sikora, 5 Things You Never Knew About Fear (Northwestern Medicine). On fear as a survival response, and how it impairs the brain’s reasoning and judgment when it spikes.

We have seen this panic before

  • Dora Czerna, Disruption Has a Shape. A designer tracing the recurring arc of technological disruption, democratization, panic, quality collapse, then new norms.
  • Calestous Juma, Why Do People Resist New Technologies? (World Economic Forum). A Harvard professor on six hundred years of fear and resistance to new technology, from coffee to electricity.
  • Derek Thompson, Why America’s AI Discourse Feels So Broken. On history as the strongest argument that AI won’t cause an overnight jobs apocalypse.
  • Nancy Koehn, Leadership Under Pressure (Harvard Business School). On research showing most leaders turn closed-minded and reactive in a crisis, and why the steady ones are rare.

The calm that wins is earned

  • Ethan Mollick, Doing Stuff with AI (One Useful Thing). On why the people who get their hands on AI, and learn its edges firsthand, stop fearing it and start using it well.
  • Patrick Neeman, AI Wants Builders. On trading the vague fear of falling behind for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work.
  • Rafat Ali, The New Skift. The Skift founder’s argument that AI makes information cheaper and judgment more valuable, and that knowledge, a point of view, and access never get cheaper.

The future is a design problem

  • Vibhas Ratanjee and Gallup, Your Most AI-Fluent Employees Are the Most Afraid. On how believing your job will be eliminated measurably drops engagement and raises burnout, often before the technology does anything.
  • David Autor, on treating the AI future as a design problem rather than a prediction exercise, and the enormous say we have in how it actually goes.
  • Carolyn Dewar, AI Won’t Decide the Future. Leaders Will (McKinsey, via Fortune). On judgment as the thing that can’t be outsourced, and leadership as the work of staying clear-eyed under uncertainty.

In a world of panic, calm and certainty win was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
